newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO orders new peace force to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO orders new peace force to Bosnia.

text.p: NATO ordered a new alliance-led peace force into Bosnia for 18 months on Tuesday to police a peace agreement that ended the 43-month-long war last November, diplomats said.
They said the alliance's 16 defence ministers approved the final "activation order" to the military to deploy the 25,000-30,000-strong Stabilisation Force (SFOR) at a meeting in Brussels.
"There was total agreement on the issue," said one diplomat.

The new force takes over from the current Implementation Force (IFOR) policing the Dayton peace accords on December 20 -- the day its mandate expires. An official transfer of authority ceremony will be held in Sarajevo on that day.
The 16 alliance ministers had already agreed the new force's rules of engagement, also endorsed by foreign ministers and the U.N. last week.

The new force has no new orders to track down and detain war criminals despite pressure from the Netherlands and Canada for more action on the issue which the main troop contributers fear could provoke a public backlash against the force.

"The force will continue to be heavily armed and it will have a full range of armoury and the capability both to protect itself and, if, and, as it becomes, necessary to act decisively against violations (of the peace accords)," Walter Slocombe, U.S. Defence Under-Secretary for Policy, earlier told reporters.

President Bill Clinton has tentatively offered some 8,000 U.S. troops to the new force which will number between 25,000-30,000 soldiers and sees the deployment of German combat troops for the first time since World War Two.
SFOR, in which 17 non-NATO countries contributing to IFOR have also agreed to take part, was authorised by a U.N. Security Council resolution last week.
Russia agreed to take part after it was closely involved in planning the mission.

Five years after it refused to send troops to join the American-led coalition in the Gulf War, the German parliament approved the deployment of up to about 2,000 peacekeeping soldiers for Bosnia last Friday.
German troops took part in IFOR, but only in logistical, engineering and medical roles and they were based in Croatia. German pilots also helped enforce the "no-fly" zone over Bosnia.

Germany's allies in Europe have been keen for Bonn to match its economic weight with a more high profile political and military role, but the country's Nazi past has limited its ability to take part in "out of theatre" NATO operations.
But in a sign of how Germany sees a future military role, the German troops will operate jointly with French forces in south-eastern Bosnia in an existing Franco-German brigade.

The ministers, who will be joined on Wednesday by Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, also reviewed ways of making the alliance's command structures more flexible and enable it to carry out more Bosnia-style peace missions.
But British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo warned his NATO allies a freefall in defence spending risked undermining the western defence alliance's capability to act in a host of areas.
NATO officials quoted Portillo as saying that European defence budgets had dropped to 1.9 percent of gross national product and only 14 percent of that went on purchases for modernisation.
The officials said Portillo -- backed by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry -- said that Europe could only forge a common defence identity as long as it had a defence capability.

The ministers also expressed concern over the proliferation of nuclear, chemical and biological weapons and "their means of delivery" and requested member states to plan for counter-measures in future defence planning.

On Wednesday, NATO hopes Rodionov will agree to build on cooperation achieved during the planning for SFOR by exchanging military liaison officers between their respective political and military commands.
On Monday, U.S. General John Shalikashvili on Monday called for a special police force to be set up to arrest war crimes suspects in Bosnia, saying it was not a job for the NATO-led peace force.
But he said a separate police force should be formed to go after indicted war criminals who have not been handed over as required by the Dayton peace accords.

"I think a way must be found where a police force can be constituted that would take care in those instances where the signatories to the (agreement) continue to refuse to turn over those war criminals," Shalikashvili said.
